CVS Group plc (CVSG-GB): investment memo

CVS Group: the bought earnings growth is predictable and the stock is cheap, but a re-rating needs two company events, most likely between March and September 2027

Date: 3 November 2026. Price: 1315p (29 Oct 2026). Market capitalisation: about £893m. Enterprise value: about £1,051m. Fiscal year: to 30 June. Next events: Bank of England rate decision, 5 Nov; Pets at Home interim results, 25 Nov; CVS four-month trading update with the annual general meeting, late November; CVS half-year trading update, January; CVS interim results, 4 Mar 2027; chief executive appointment, undated. The earnings basis, forecasts of record and sources are set out in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The verdict for RichardCVS's earnings case is sound and the stock is cheap, but the risk/reward is not yet unusually skewed to the positive. The skew is likely to appear between March and September 2027, after three soft results prints, unless the appointment of a credible chief executive arrives first and pulls the window forward.

What CVS is. CVS Group is a veterinary consolidator in the UK (about 89 percent of revenue) and Australia (about 11 percent). It owns over 400 UK practices, 61 Australian sites, three reference laboratories and an online pharmacy, Animed.

How CVS's earnings grow. CVS has two engines, and only one of them is running. The UK organic engine has stalled in volume and grows only through price. The capital-allocation engine is producing near-mechanical adjusted EPS growth of 9 to 11 percent a year, after three years of decline. That engine has three parts: a £50m share buyback that is nearly complete; about £50m a year of acquisitions, at about 6x EBITDA in Australia and through a reopened UK pipeline; and bank leverage raised to 1.63x EBITDA.

The eight things that matter.

  1. 1

    CVS's earnings are predictable; its share price is not.

    About 60 percent of FY2027's EPS growth comes from the lower share count, which the buyback has already delivered. Most of the remaining growth comes from acquired EBITDA that CVS already owns or has signed. The UK organic practices contribute almost nothing net, and CVS can deliver consensus within a few percent without them. Our plausible range for FY2027 EPS is about 82p to 104p around a base of 93p, with a 60 percent chance of landing within 5 percent of the base. That range is narrow for a UK consumer-facing mid-cap. The share price, by contrast, depends on two company events that cannot be forecast (point 4).

  2. 2

    The next three results prints will look worse than the underlying business.

    Group like-for-like (LFL) revenue growth will print about 1.5 percent in the November and January updates, against 2.7 percent a year earlier. The slowdown comes from Animed and the laboratories, which supplied half of FY2026's 2.1 percent group LFL growth and are now normalising. UK practice LFL growth is actually improving, from 1.0 percent to about 1.4 percent. The first-half (H1) EBITDA margin will be flat and the second-half (H2) margin down about half a point, because the FY2026 research and development (R&D) expenditure credit included a £6.6m one-off release that no covering broker in our files has written about. Our FY2027 forecasts sit 1 to 2 percent below consensus for reasons that are facts in the annual report, not forecasts.

  3. 3

    There is no cushion of conservative guidance to unlock.

    CVS gives no profit guidance. It points investors at consensus, meets consensus once consensus has been cut, and has never raised guidance. CVS has missed its medium-term framework of 4 to 8 percent LFL growth three years running. The incoming chief executive is more likely to reset that framework (about 60 percent probability within a year of appointment) than to meet it.

  4. 4

    A re-rating needs two company events, not a sector tide.

    About 87 percent of the variation in CVS's share price is specific to CVS; its beta to a basket of care peers is about 0.5. The P/E multiple sits at the 13th percentile of its ten-year history because of two CVS-specific worries: a flat organic engine and an empty chief executive's chair. Only CVS-specific events can resolve those worries: the appointment of a credible chief executive, and an LFL growth print of 3 percent or more. The best chance of such a print is H2 FY2027, which faces an easy comparative because heat depressed the prior year's fourth quarter.

  5. 5

    CVS's out-years are better than consensus recognises.

    Consensus FY2029 earnings hold only if acquisitions continue, yet brokers either omit future acquisitions (Jefferies) or model them without saying so. Our FY2029 forecasts are 5 percent above consensus for revenue and 3.6 percent above for EBITDA, and our FY2030 EPS is 14 percent above a consensus figure drawn from only two brokers. Consensus also under-models the fall in the share count: consensus net income divided by consensus EPS implies about 68.5m shares, against 66.3m once the buyback completes. A renewal of the buyback (about 55 percent probability within twelve months of the appointment) is not in the price.

  6. 6

    The downside is bounded and cushioned by private-market value.

    At a fair trough multiple of 10.9x (the ten-year 10th percentile) on consensus earnings, CVS shares would be worth about 1,150p (−13 percent); on earnings 7 percent below consensus, about 1,070p (−19 percent). The 52-week low of 1,062p corroborates that level. Private buyers paid about 9x EBITDA for Spire Healthcare in September 2026; at 9x FY2027 EBITDA CVS's equity is worth about 1,770p, and at 10x about 1,990p. An activist investor, Converium, is on the shareholder register, and the laboratories could be sold separately (Deutsche Bank values them at over £100m).

  7. 7

    Two-thirds of the modelled return comes from the multiple.

    At the guideline fair multiple of 14.92x, the model gives a total shareholder return of +37.8 percent to December 2027 (the 18-month column): +9.3 points from earnings, +25.3 from the multiple and +0.7 from dividends. To June 2029 the modelled return is +64.8 percent. We can defend the earnings leg, about 9 to 11 percent a year, on transacted facts. The multiple leg rests on the two events in point 4, which the next six months are more likely to test than to deliver.

  8. 8

    The practical implication: the entry point the framework looks for is more likely to arrive between March and September 2027 than today.

    By March 2027 the three soft prints will be behind CVS, the comparatives will ease, the FY2026 and FY2027 acquisitions will have annualised, the chief executive will probably be named, the first data on the Healthy Pet Club Advanced tier will be out, and the out-year arithmetic will become visible. Only the appointment, which is undated and could come at any time, could pull that window forward. A step-down in UK volume of more than a point as published prices bite would close the window, and the January update would reveal it.

Where we differ from the market. We are below consensus in the near term and above it in the out-years. We are below on FY2027 EBITDA because the £6.6m R&D release does not repeat, and above on FY2029 and FY2030 revenue and EBITDA because we model the acquisitions CVS says it will make. We expect the market to read the November and January headlines as deceleration while the UK practice trend is improving. The sell-side has bought the re-rating (73 percent Buy ratings, median target price 1,600p) without the estimates to support it, so the near-term breadth of estimate revisions is likely to tip negative. We agree with the market that organic growth is price-led and that Australia, where CVS buys practices at about 6x EBITDA, is the growth engine. We think the market under-weights how far published prices now worsen the trade-off between price and volume, and over-weights the chance that a sector re-rating reaches CVS by osmosis.

Scorecard: topics 1 to 12

#1 Operating environment: tailwinds, headwinds and risks

CVS's external picture has moved from hostile to merely unhelpful: regulation and labour no longer hurt, but the 2027 UK consumer squeeze will hold UK volume down for the next 6 to 12 months.

Regulation: the largest headwind of the last three years has gone. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) issued its final decision on 24 Mar 2026 and its binding order on 22 Sep 2026. Both impose transparency remedies only: online price lists, ownership branding, written estimates above £500, prescription rights, and a £21 cap on written prescriptions that sits at the market average. The CMA imposed no divestments and no caps on service prices. CVS's UK acquisition pipeline has reopened with a £15m two-site deal.

Labour: vet availability has turned from a constraint into modest support. The vet vacancy rate fell to 5.8 percent, from 6.5 percent a year earlier and 9.3 percent in FY2024. Applicants per role have risen, EU vets are returning, and the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons models no medium-term shortage. CVS's clinical staff costs fell to 34.3 percent of revenue in H2 FY2026, from 36.0 percent. The April 2027 rise in the wage floor is known and modest (+3.9 percent to £13.21), and the 28 Oct 2026 Budget added no new employer-tax step.

The consumer: 2027 is the UK consumer's weak year. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecasts UK growth of 1.0 percent, inflation peaking near 3.75 percent and Bank Rate at about 4.25 percent by mid-2027; the energy price cap rises about 16 percent in January. Some 45 percent of households are limiting non-essential purchases, and UK pet spending fell 1 percent in 2025. US clinic visits have fallen for 18 consecutive quarters (−2.2 percent in the third quarter of 2026), and Piper Sandler expects UK visits to be flat to down 1 percent in 2027.

Veterinary demand is splitting in two. Reactive, referral and diagnostic demand is holding: CVS's laboratory volumes rose 4.3 percent and laboratory EBITDA 25.6 percent. Routine wellness visits, preventive bloodwork and elective work are being deferred. Medicines are leaking to online pharmacies, which are 50 to 60 percent cheaper and now have a regulatory nudge from the CMA's prescription remedies.

Two slower forces help. The pandemic pet cohort, about 2m UK pets now aged four to six, enters its higher-need years from about age five, which helps FY2028 more than FY2027. In the capital market, private buyers are paying 9x to 14x EBITDA for European healthcare assets, against CVS's 7x.

Inference. The external forces that remain are moderate, identifiable and mostly already in the base forecasts. The tail risk that drove the 2023 to 2025 de-rating, structural regulation, has gone. External forces will permit about 2 to 3 percent organic growth; they will not drive the case. The one powerful external force in the investor's favour, private-market valuation, supports the equity value rather than the earnings.

So what. Model no external tailwind to UK volume in FY2027 (we carry a 2.5 percent fall), a gradual tailwind in FY2028 and FY2029 as the pandemic cohort ages, and price as the only organic lever. CVS's cost base needs price rises of 3 to 4 percent a year just to stand still. Treat the gap to private-market valuations as a floor under the shares and an option on a bid, not as a forecast.

Strongest counter-case. The consumer squeeze is sharper than the OBR's central case, and published prices turn the slow leakage of medicines into a visible loss of elective and routine work to independent practices, which charge about £20 to £25 less per consultation. UK volume then falls 3.5 to 4 percent rather than 2.5 percent, and the squeeze hits the margin, not just revenue. That scenario is the downside leg of our FY2027 range (EPS about 82p), and reaching it needs nothing outside recent experience: FY2025 was such a year.

What would change my view. Two pieces of evidence would move the external picture from headwind to neutral a year early. The first is a January update or March interim results showing UK practice LFL growth above 2 percent driven by volume rather than price, with membership rising and the clinical staff ratio steady. The second is a Pets at Home vet print on 25 Nov showing UK volume turning. Conversely, Healthy Pet Club membership falling below about 500,000 would show that price transparency is biting harder than modelled.

Against the market. The sell-side knows the direction of all these forces (price-led growth, weak footfall, the pandemic cohort, Australia), and we agree with it. We differ in two respects. First, neither covering house has sized the effect of published prices on elective work. Second, the prevailing narrative still treats the CMA clearing as a tailwind yet to be rewarded; we think the market has already priced the clearing, and its concern has moved on to the organic engine and the empty chief executive's chair.

Conclusion: the operating environment is a modest and identifiable net headwind for the next 6 to 12 months, clearly less adverse than in the last three years, with a slow structural tailwind from FY2028 and a strong valuation tailwind that reaches the equity only through a bid or through CVS's own numbers.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. The CMA tail risk is gone (transparency remedies only) and labour has turned supportive (vacancies 5.8%, clinical staff 34.3% of revenue), but the UK consumer squeeze of 2027, deferral of routine and elective work, online medicine leakage and published prices leave a modest net headwind to volume for 6-12 months, with the pet-cohort tailwind only from FY2028 and the private-market valuation gap helping the equity, not earnings; consensus sales growth at the 46th percentile is a fair read, and the company sits just above Indutrade's soft-demand backdrop, coherent with the group's 43.

#2 Internal change forces and their risks

CVS is changing its capital allocation, not its operations, and the change that matters most, the choice of the next chief executive, has not yet happened.

The defining internal change is a vacancy. Chief executive Richard Fairman announced his retirement on 30 Mar 2026. A board succession sub-committee formed on 22 Jul 2026 and appointed an external search firm. Seven months after the announcement no successor is named, and Fairman stays until one is.

Almost everything around the vacancy has moved. CVS has hired a Chief Operating Officer from IVC Evidensia, put a Chief Veterinary Officer on the board, appointed its first Australian Managing Director and is recruiting a Chief Client Officer. The board has three new non-executive directors and a new Senior Independent Director. An activist, Converium (2 percent economic stake), demanded a £100m buyback in a letter of 13 May 2026; CVS answered with a £50m programme thirteen days later.

The capital-allocation changes are real, funded and executing (Figure 6). CVS bought back £20m of shares by January 2026, then launched the £50m programme in May 2026, which is about three-quarters done. Acquisition spending rose to £45.8m in FY2026, and the target is about £50m a year, allocated "dynamically" between the UK and Australia; UK acquisitions restarted after a two-year pause. A new £350m bank facility runs to May 2030 at a margin 20 basis points lower than before. Bank leverage has risen from 1.18x to 1.63x EBITDA, and CVS has said it is willing to exceed its 2.0x guardrail temporarily for acquisitions.

Standards have improved measurably in cost discipline and governance. The cost discipline shows in rostering, retendered procurement contracts and capital expenditure cut from £36.4m to about £30m. The governance improvement shows in the move to the Main Market, membership of the FTSE 250 and independent board committees.

The organic initiatives are sensible and small. The Healthy Pet Club Advanced tier signed about 14,500 clients in three months. Clients have booked over 150,000 appointments online. A national CVS Vets brand now covers over 80 percent of practices, nurses now do dental work, and an artificial-intelligence note-taking scribe is in trial.

CVS has not raised guidance, and two signals point the wrong way. CVS reaffirmed its 4 to 8 percent LFL framework after delivering 2.9, 0.2 and 2.1 percent in the last three years. Its ambition to double adjusted EBITDA slipped quietly from FY2027 to FY2028, where consensus (£158m) says the target is out of reach. Executive base salaries rose 14 to 19 percent from July 2026, after a three-year total shareholder return of −22 percent. Employee engagement appears to have fallen in H2 FY2026: the engagement score was +10.0 in December 2025 and +5.8 for the full year.

Inference. CVS is changing its capital allocation, not its operations. The financial forces (the buyback, acquisitions in two countries, higher leverage and cost discipline) make EPS growth of 9 to 10 percent in FY2027 close to arithmetic before any organic recovery. The operating initiatives are untested, and we credit them with no more than half a point of LFL growth until they show in membership and volume. The change that would most alter the trajectory, the new chief executive, is a vacancy whose direction is unknown. The board's language ("requisite operational skills") says it wants an operator rather than another finance-track capital allocator. Peer precedents show that a new chief executive more often than not resets targets, takes charges or re-cuts capital returns within twelve months.

So what. Carry the capital-allocation mechanics in full. Treat a renewal of the buyback after the £50m programme completes as a mild upside rather than a given: we put about 55 percent probability on a £20m to £30m renewal within a year of the appointment, worth about 1 percent of FY2028 EPS. Carry a reset by the new chief executive, in H2 FY2027 to H1 FY2028, as a risk to the medium-term targets and to the narrative, not to consensus EBITDA, which already assumes only 2.5 to 3 percent organic growth. The market is as likely to receive such a reset well as badly; a good reception would follow a credible 3 to 5 percent LFL range, a buyback policy and a quantified cost programme of £8m to £12m.

Strongest counter-case. The successor is a caretaker or another finance-track hire who prefers reinvestment to buybacks (Jefferies' stated preference) and slows Australian acquisitions as private-equity bidding pushes multiples for premium practices towards 9x to 10x EBITDA, and the activist exits. CVS's mechanical EPS growth then fades to 5 to 6 percent a year from FY2028, and the multiple has no trigger.

What would change my view. The first trigger is the appointment announcement itself. A respected multi-site healthcare operator with clinical credibility would move our grade for internal change forces from D towards C in a day; a caretaker would confirm the D. The second trigger is the new chief executive's first strategy update: on our arithmetic, a stated buyback policy and a cost programme would be worth 6 to 9 percent of EPS by FY2029.

Against the market. The market knows about the vacancy and the buyback, and both covering houses discuss them, but nobody sizes the reset or the buyback renewal. We think the market under-weights how likely the new chief executive is to cut the LFL target (we say 60 percent) and how little such a cut matters to consensus earnings, and under-weights the chance of a buyback renewal. We agree with Jefferies that leverage approaching 2.0x limits the scale of further returns while £50m a year goes on acquisitions.

Conclusion: internal change at CVS is strong, funded and executing on capital allocation, but narrow and untested on operations, and the most important change, the choice of chief executive, is a binary event still to come.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The capital-allocation change is large, funded and executing (the £50m buyback cutting average shares about 5.5%, £50m a year of deals at about 6x in Australia plus a reopened UK pipeline, leverage raised to 1.63x, capex cut), turning EPS from three years of decline to 9-11% growth, but operations are untouched (initiatives worth under half a point of LFL), targets have slipped and the chief executive chair is empty; I weigh the funded mechanics as a net positive where the Analyst reads D, close to Odfjell's deal-and-refinancing positives and coherent with the group's 58.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

CVS stands on a strong industry structure but holds an ordinary competitive position: its earnings base is mid-quality, and its management allocates capital well without having compounded per-share value.

Industry structure: UK first-opinion care is a concentrated, rational oligopoly that puts margin first. Corporate groups own about 60 percent of UK practices, up from 10 percent in 2013, and the top five groups own about 45 percent. The six groups under the same regulatory spotlight have behaved alike: they set prices centrally in percentile bands, and they raised prices about 5 percent a year through three years of falling volume. The CMA's 30 percent ceiling on local market share caps further UK concentration.

CVS is a mid-sized UK player. CVS is number two or three in the UK, with 8 to 9 percent of practices. It is far behind IVC Evidensia, whose EBITDA of about £720m is five times CVS's. It is level with Pets at Home's joint-venture network, whose vet consumer revenue of £688m compares with CVS's UK practice revenue of about £569m.

Australia is the opposite of the UK: fragmented and open to consolidation. Corporate groups own only 15 to 20 percent of Australia's 3,600 to 3,800 practices; VetPartners has 7 percent, Greencross 6 percent and CVS 1 to 2 percent. About 40 percent of the 1,100 metropolitan practices meet CVS's acquisition criteria.

Business model: CVS's advantages are real but ordinary, and none is unique. CVS has four advantages:

  • The Healthy Pet Club: 508,000 members (−2.1 percent), £95.5m of recurring revenue (+3.5 percent), and over 40 percent of active patients.
  • Three laboratories with an overnight courier fleet: half their volume comes from external clinics, at margins above 30 percent.
  • Procurement scale: non-clinical cost of sales is 21.4 percent of revenue.
  • A proven Australian acquisition capability: 61 sites bought in three years at about 6x EBITDA, practices performing ahead of their business cases, and immediate synergies from moving each practice to a single wholesaler.

The advantaged UK model belongs to Pets at Home, not to CVS. Pets at Home's joint-venture practices are part-owned by their vets and price close to independent practices. Their clinician turnover is 27 percent, and their consumer revenue grew 6.3 percent in FY2026, against CVS's UK practice LFL growth of 1.0 percent. The CMA found that corporate groups priced 18.3 percent above independents, and that gap is now published.

Online pharmacies can substitute only for medicines. Goods are about 30 percent of practice revenue, and most chronic medicine sales have already moved online. Consultations, surgery, diagnostics and emergencies, about 70 percent of practice revenue, have no substitute.

Financial profile: CVS's margin sits at the bottom of its target range, and about 2 points of it is a tax credit. The adjusted EBITDA margin has been 19.7 to 20.0 percent for three years, at the bottom of the 19 to 23 percent target range. About 2.2 points of that margin is the R&D expenditure credit; excluding the credit, the margin is 17.65 percent, down from 18.4 percent in FY2023. FactSet's adjusted EBIT margin is about 10.6 percent.

Returns on capital roughly match CVS's hurdle. Pre-tax return on capital employed (ROCE) is 16.1 percent (17.3 percent the year before), or about 12 percent after tax, against a 12 percent internal hurdle. The blended return on the £228m deployed since FY2023 has been low, because wage inflation and one-off shocks absorbed the EBITDA that CVS bought.

Cash conversion and debt are comfortable. Adjusted operating cash conversion was 70.6 percent (76.9 percent the year before), and company free cash flow was £69.2m. Net bank debt is £199.6m, or 1.63x EBITDA on the bank-covenant test (2.16x including leases, on FactSet's basis). Interest cover is 13.1x, and the leverage covenant is 3.25x.

CVS's earnings base is not clean. Adjusted profit before tax was £84.9m against reported profit before tax of £32.0m. Business combination costs of £14.8m a year recur with the acquisition model but sit outside adjusted earnings. Those costs include £10.5m of contingent consideration that CVS must expense because the payments are tied to the vendors' continued employment, plus deal fees. The reported tax rate is 44.4 percent, and reported EPS was 24.4p against adjusted EPS of 85.6p.

Management: a disciplined, honest, finance-led capital allocator. Management sold the Crematoria business at about 10x EBITDA (May 2025) and recycled the proceeds into Australian practices at about 6x. It exited the Netherlands and Ireland, paused UK acquisitions for two years while the regulator decided, refinanced early, and bought back shares at an 8 percent earnings yield against an after-tax cost of debt of about 4 percent. CVS executed every capital action it announced in the last 18 months.

Management's operating record is weaker than its capital record. CVS missed its organic targets three years running, and adjusted EPS fell from 95.5p (FY2023) to 85.6p (FY2026) while revenue grew 21 percent. Pets at Home grew its vet division faster through the same conditions. The chief financial officer, in post since 2019, anchors the finance function, but the top team is thin: CVS has had no Deputy Chief Executive since 2024, and the Chief Client Officer post is unfilled. Executive incentives are 80 percent based on adjusted EBITDA, which the acquisition model can buy.

Inference. CVS's industry structure is its strongest foundation, and its position in the value chain its weakest. The business is mid-quality and stable rather than strong and improving. Management allocates capital well at the margin but has not compounded per-share value. Organic share in UK first-opinion care is consolidating in the joint-venture model, not in the fully corporate model that CVS runs.

So what. Price, procurement and the mix shift to Australia defend CVS's margin (adding about 0.1 to 0.2 points a year); no competitive moat expands it. Without acquisitions, CVS's UK organic market share drifts slightly down. Trust the company's capital execution and its near-term numbers; do not trust its medium-term organic targets. Track reported EPS (about 42p in FY2027) and a cash measure alongside adjusted EPS, because a market that re-based its valuation to reported earnings would see a much higher multiple.

Strongest counter-case. Three facts would argue for stronger foundations. The laboratories, referral hospitals and procurement form an integrated chain that Deutsche Bank calls CVS's moat. Australian practices bought at 6x EBITDA reach returns on capital of 19 to 23 percent within three to five years. And nurse pay, clinical pathways and lower vacancies are fixing the corporate model's staff-retention problem. On that reading CVS's foundations deserve a B, not a C.

What would change my view. Any of three disclosures: clinician turnover below 30 percent, Healthy Pet Club membership turning up, or two consecutive halves of UK practice margin expansion excluding the R&D credit.

Against the market. We agree with the market on the industry structure and on the economics of Australian acquisitions. We think the market under-weights two issues: contingent consideration recurs, so about a third of the adjusted EPS accretion from acquisitions is not economic; and the R&D credit props up the margin. We also think the market over-rates CVS's laboratories as a moat relative to the joint-venture model's advantages in clinician retention and price perception.

Conclusion: CVS has a supportive industry structure, an ordinary competitive position, a mid-quality financial profile with a policy-exposed tax credit inside the margin, and a competent finance-led management whose successor matters more than its record.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. A rational, defensive UK oligopoly with an Australian runway (group 60) carries ordinary, non-unique advantages (group 50) and a finance-led management that has not grown per-share value through three years of organic misses (group 44); the figures confirm a weak economic profile (ROIC 3.1%, 23rd percentile; EBITDA margin median at 52nd but holding about 2 points of R&D credit; adjusted PBT 2.7x reported with recurring contingent consideration; low return on the £228m deployed since FY2023), so it sits just above IMCD, which has falling EPS but a stronger moat, and below Munters.

#4 Conservatism of guidance, expectation management and the record of delivery

CVS is an honest tracker, not a sandbagger: it meets consensus only after consensus has been cut, so no hidden cushion exists, and the likeliest guidance event is a reset by the new chief executive.

What CVS guides. CVS gives no numeric EBITDA or EPS guidance. At the FY2026 results on 24 Sep 2026 it said trading was in line, with positive early LFL growth, and expressed comfort with consensus FY2027 EBITDA of £149.0m to £151.7m and EPS of about 94.9p. It also reaffirmed its medium-term framework: LFL growth of 4 to 8 percent, an EBITDA margin of 19 to 23 percent, cash conversion above 70 percent, leverage below 2.0x, capital expenditure of about £30m, and acquisitions of about £50m a year.

CVS's record against consensus is one of meeting numbers only after they have been cut (Figure 13). EBITDA missed consensus by 2.2 percent in FY2024 because of a cyber attack. EBITDA beat consensus by 2.7 percent in FY2025, but only after Deutsche Bank had cut its EPS forecast by 6 percent, and a £2.3m rise in the R&D credit made the beat. H1 FY2026 missed by 2.7 percent. FY2026 came in line, after a 12 percent cut to FY2026 consensus EPS in October 2025.

Consensus has already done its cutting (Figure 14). FY2026 consensus EPS fell from 101p to 85.8p over its forecast life, and FY2027 consensus EPS fell from 107p to 95p, almost all of it in 2024 and 2025. Over the last six months, FY2027 consensus EPS has moved within a 1 percent band.

The sell-side is more bullish on ratings than on numbers. Seven of nine brokers rate CVS Buy or Overweight, and two rate it Hold (Jefferies, target 1,400p; Shore Capital, target 1,250p). Target prices range from 1,250p to 1,900p, with a median of 1,600p, 22 percent above the share price. The share of Buy ratings is 73 percent, up 9 points in six months.

Inference. CVS is an honest tracker, neither a sandbagger nor an upgrader. It sets near-term numbers at consensus and meets them once consensus has been cut; its misses are concentrated in first halves; and it reaffirmed its medium-term targets through three years of misses before letting them slip quietly. Estimates have done their cutting and are now realistic (they assume only 2.5 to 3 percent organic growth), which limits downside revisions, but there is no cushion. The departing chief executive has no incentive to raise anything, and the successor is more likely to reset the targets than to raise them.

So what. We assign the following probabilities (Figure 16). For FY2027: the outcome lands inside, or within 2 percent of, the comfort range, about 60 percent; CVS trims its expectation to the bottom of the range or slightly below before September 2027, about 30 percent; CVS raises it, about 10 percent. The most likely form of a trim is a "towards the lower end" comment in January or March, not a profit warning. For the medium term: CVS raises any target, below 10 percent; CVS resets the LFL range within a year of the appointment, about 60 percent; CVS drops or replaces the FY2028 EBITDA-doubling ambition, about 80 percent.

Strongest counter-case. Management's informal tone is more positive than consensus on the organic and Australian stories. Management has "high confidence" in a return to 4 to 8 percent LFL growth, says Australian practices are "ahead of plans", and disclosed Australian LFL growth of 3.0 percent for FY2026. A repeat provision release (£2.9m of the provision remains) plus a summer price rise "slightly above historical rates" could produce a beat in July 2027. Management's tone, however, has been a fair predictor of near-term profit and a poor predictor of organic delivery.

What would change my view. Either of two breaks with the pattern: a four-month update showing group LFL growth above 3 percent, or a new chief executive who chooses to start with forecasts above consensus.

Against the market. The market reads CVS's "comfort with consensus" as a floor; we read it as the number itself, and we think the R&D release and the tough comparative make the bottom of the range the likelier landing. We agree with Deutsche Bank that estimates face little downside; we add that they face little upside either.

Conclusion: CVS's guidance is neither conservative nor sandbagged, its record is of meeting cut numbers and missing organic targets, and the likeliest guidance event in the next twelve months is a reset of the framework by the new chief executive rather than a raise.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. An honest tracker that meets numbers only after they have been cut (FY2026 EPS consensus 101p to 85.8p, FY2027 107p to 95p; H1 FY2026 and FY2024 misses; the FY2025 beat made by the R&D credit), has never raised guidance, reaffirmed the 4-8% LFL framework through three years of misses and let the EBITDA-doubling ambition slip a year, with current comfort sitting at consensus and no cushion; a two-to-three-year record of target misses weighs heavily, coherent with the groups' 40 and 46.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

CVS turns revenue growth into outsized EPS growth through the share count, the acquisition spread and below-EBITDA arithmetic, not through pricing power or operating leverage, which stay dormant until UK volume turns.

Price: CVS can pass costs through, but only at the expense of volume. UK practice revenue rose about 0.9 percent in FY2026 while volume fell about 3 to 4 percent, so price rose about 4 to 5 percent. Healthy Pet Club revenue per member rose about 5 to 6 percent, and the summer 2026 price rises were "slightly above historical rates". Yet employment costs still rose as a share of revenue (from 52.2 to 52.3 percent) despite rostering, and the margin excluding the R&D credit fell 0.75 points over three years of 3 to 5 percent price rises.

Price competition is intensifying. A consultation costs about £70 to £75 at a corporate practice against about £50 at an independent, and the CMA's finding that corporates price 18.3 percent above independents is now public. IVC Evidensia (1m Pet Health Club members, plus a Plus tier with unlimited consultations) and Medivet (10 percent off all bills; £100 vaccinations for life) are bundling aggressively.

Operating leverage: staff make up two-thirds of the UK practice cost base. Under the IFRS 16 lease accounting standard, rent sits below EBITDA. The UK practice cost base above EBITDA (about £466m) is therefore about two-thirds staff (about £305m), a quarter drugs and consumables (about £120m) and the rest other costs. A service price rise drops through to EBITDA at 95 to 100 percent. Lost volume drops through at about 75 percent in the first months and about 50 percent once rosters flex; FY2026 showed that flex, with clinical staff costs falling from 36.0 to 34.3 percent of revenue in H2.

The precedent often cited for a volume-driven margin jump is mostly an accounting effect. Most of the 4-point margin jump in H1 FY2020 came from adopting IFRS 16; the underlying operating leverage was 0.5 to 1 point. The one segment with clear positive operating leverage is the laboratories: revenue growth of 11.5 percent became EBITDA growth of 25.6 percent, an incremental margin of about 64 percent (we use 45 percent in our forecasts).

Financial leverage: the buyback and acquisitions add EPS directly. The £50m buyback cuts FY2027 average diluted shares by about 5.5 percent, from 71.0m to 67.3m; net of the interest lost on the cash spent, the buyback adds about 3 percent to EPS. Each year's £50m of acquisitions at 6.6x to 7.5x EBITDA buys £7.5m to £8m of EBITDA. After about £1.5m of depreciation and lease cost, about £3.2m of interest and 29 percent tax, each year's acquisitions add about 3.3p to 3.6p of EPS on an annualised basis.

CVS's interest-rate sensitivity doubles from 2028. Bank debt costs about 6 percent all-in. CVS has swapped £100m into a fixed 3.83 percent until February 2028; after that, all of the roughly £240m of bank debt floats. A 1-point move in SONIA (the Sterling Overnight Index Average, the floating benchmark rate) costs about 0.9p of EPS now and about 1.8p from FY2029.

Cost scope: no programme is announced, and routine savings only offset wage rises. Rostering took out cost worth 1.7 points of revenue, and that saving is banked. Further productivity gains (nurses doing dental work, artificial-intelligence scribes, fewer locums) are worth 0.3 to 0.6 percent of staff cost a year, and procurement savings 0.1 to 0.2 points of revenue; the April wage steps absorb both. A new chief executive could target £8m to £12m of savings (1 to 1.5 points of margin) across the support office, procurement, Animed and pricing architecture, at an exceptional cost of £4m to £8m over 12 to 24 months. Pets at Home's £20m programme, announced in November 2025, took about 15 months.

Feedback loops: two loops dominate CVS's trajectory (Figure 18). The reinforcing capital-allocation loop works like this: recovering free cash flow and leverage headroom fund about £50m a year of acquisitions and buybacks; each annual cohort of acquisitions adds £7.5m to £8m of EBITDA; and that EBITDA funds the next round. The capital-allocation loop supplies about 70 percent of EBITDA growth to FY2031 and lifts Australia from about one-seventh of EBITDA before central costs to about a quarter.

The balancing UK price-and-volume loop works the other way: price rises cause clients to defer routine care and members to churn; volume falls 2 to 3 percent; fixed staff costs then pressure the next price rise; and published prices make clients more sensitive to each rise. The price-and-volume loop caps UK practice LFL growth at 1.5 to 2.5 percent until FY2029.

Inference. CVS has nominal pricing power, which passes cost through at the expense of volume, not real pricing power, which expands margins. Operating leverage is dormant until UK volume turns, which we expect in FY2030. What lifts the group margin by 0.1 to 0.2 points a year is mix (Australia at about a 25 percent margin, the laboratories at 33 to 36 percent), not operating leverage. Financial leverage adds about 3 points to FY2027 EPS growth and 1.5 to 2.5 points a year thereafter. Revenue growth therefore produces outsized EPS growth, with EPS compounding 2 to 4 points a year faster than EBITDA, for financial reasons rather than operating ones.

So what. Three UK drivers set our FY2027 earnings range (Figure 19); in FY2027, each £1m of EBITDA is worth about 1.06p of EPS. One point of UK price is worth about £5.8m of EBITDA and 6.2p of EPS. One point of UK volume is worth about £2.9m and 3.1p once rosters flex, or 4.6p before they flex. One point of UK wage inflation is worth £3.1m to £3.7m and 3.3p to 3.9p. The combination that matters is price minus wages minus half of any volume loss: about +0.4 points in FY2027 and about zero in FY2028 and FY2029.

Strongest counter-case. The Healthy Pet Club Advanced tier (unlimited consultations) and the ageing pandemic cohort turn UK volume flat a year earlier than modelled. The 50 percent drop-through then works upwards, and each point of volume is worth 3p to 5p of EPS at no extra cost. The laboratories show what the group would look like with volume growth. That scenario is the upside leg of our FY2027 range (EPS about 104p).

What would change my view. A clinical staff ratio holding at or below 34 percent of revenue while practice LFL growth exceeds 2 percent would show that operating leverage has turned positive; a ratio above 34.5 percent would show that wages are winning again.

Against the market. Deutsche Bank expects price to contribute more to organic growth after the summer rises and sees margins stable. We agree on the mechanism, but we think the volume penalty for each price rise is now larger than in 2022 to 2023, because every price is online. AlphaSense's downside arithmetic (180 to 220 basis points of margin lost per 1 percent of volume) implies a drop-through above 300 percent, and we reject it.

Conclusion: CVS's business model converts revenue into outsized EPS growth through the share count, the acquisition spread and below-EBITDA arithmetic rather than through pricing power or operating leverage, which stay dormant until UK volume turns.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. Pricing power is nominal (4-5% price taken but volume falls 3-4% and the ex-credit margin fell 0.75 points), operating leverage is dormant and partly works against the company (staff two-thirds of the practice cost base, lost volume dropping through at 75% then 50% once rosters flex), and no cost programme is announced (a possible £8-12m under a new chief executive); what gears EPS is financial (buyback and the acquisition spread, 2-4 points over EBITDA) and the capital-allocation loop, giving forecast EPS growth of about 1.5x revenue growth, below the Universe's typical 2x, coherent with the groups' 38 and 48.

#6 Forecast financials and the scope for faster growth than the past

Our forecasts show adjusted EPS compounding at 9 to 11 percent a year because CVS buys its growth and divides it over fewer shares, not because the operating business improves; we sit 1 to 2 percent below consensus for FY2027 and above it from FY2029.

The base case. Our forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (Figure 20). Revenue grows 6 to 7 percent a year, the EBITDA margin stays close to 20 percent, free cash flow roughly doubles from FY2026, and the share count falls every year.

The FY2027 EPS bridge: the share count is the largest source of growth, and the R&D credit is the largest drag (Figure 21). The buyback adds 4.7p, acquisitions 2.3p and organic growth with the smaller segments 2.5p; the reset of the R&D credit takes away 3.4p and higher costs below EBITDA 1.4p. Those five steps explain 4.7p of the 7.7p increase; the Analyst's bridge does not itemise the remaining 3.0p.

The assumptions behind the base case (Figure 22). The UK practices grow only through price, Australia grows through acquisitions, and the lines below EBITDA rise with the acquisitions.

The half-years the market will see first: a flat H1 margin and a lower H2 margin, both caused by the R&D credit (Figure 24). H1 FY2027 revenue should be about £377m (+5.7 percent) and EBITDA about £72.0m, a margin of 19.1 percent against 19.0 percent a year earlier. Delivering that H1 needs about 8.5 percent growth in EBITDA excluding the R&D credit, which the rollover of the Australian acquisitions supplies. H2 FY2027 revenue should be about £380m (+6.7 percent) and EBITDA about £76.8m, a margin of 20.2 percent against 20.7 percent, because the H2 FY2026 comparative held most of the £6.6m release. H1 FY2028 should show about £404m of revenue and £78m of EBITDA.

Why EPS growth can beat the past: five factors change, and none of them is the UK organic core. Our forecasts compound EPS at 9 to 11 percent a year (double digit from FY2029), against −3.6 percent a year from FY2023 to FY2026 and +6.9 percent in FY2026. Five factors explain the difference:

  • Three one-off costs do not repeat: the payroll-tax step, the cyber attack and the CMA costs.
  • The share count falls instead of rising.
  • Acquisitions are made at 6x to 7.5x EBITDA in Australia rather than at about 10x in the UK.
  • The R&D credit stops rising and steps down; it is the one item that turns from tailwind to headwind.
  • The UK organic core is unchanged, so it neither helps nor hurts.

Revenue growth of 6.2 to 7.0 percent a year is within the historical range, and the EBITDA margin moves only 0.45 points in five years. Reported EPS rises from 24.4p to about 42p in FY2027 and about 82p in FY2031, and stays 40 to 55 percent below adjusted EPS throughout.

Against consensus: below in FY2027, close in FY2028, above from FY2029 (Figure 27). For FY2027 our EBITDA is £148.8m against consensus of £150.6m (−1.0 percent), because of the R&D credit (−£3.2m) and a tough H1. Our FY2027 profit before tax is £87.9m against £91.1m (£2.2m from EBITDA plus £1.0m from D&A and interest). Our FY2027 EPS is 93.3p against 95.0p; our lower share count (67.3m, against about 68.5m implied by consensus) adds back 1.7p.

For FY2028 we are above consensus on revenue (+2.9 percent) and EBITDA (+1.4 percent) but below on EPS (−0.4 to −1.8 percent), because of a weaker UK organic margin and higher costs below EBITDA. For FY2029 we are above consensus on revenue (+5.3 percent), EBITDA (+3.6 percent) and EPS (+0.8 to +2.2 percent). For FY2030 our EPS is 14 to 16 percent above a consensus figure drawn from two brokers. The consensus D&A line (£41.1m flat, then £22.7m) and the fall in consensus FY2030 EPS are artefacts of thin broker coverage.

The key judgements, and what each is worth if wrong

Four judgements explain about 85 percent of the difference between our forecasts and the last four years. A fifth judgement, the multiple, explains most of the modelled return and is treated in #11. The base for every sensitivity below is FY2027 EPS of 93.3p, and each £1m of EBITDA is worth about 1.06p of EPS.

Judgement 1: UK practice volume falls 2.5 percent in FY2027 and recovers only with the pandemic cohort, not with CVS's initiatives. If volume falls 4.0 percent instead (the FY2025-style outcome), the extra 1.5 points on about £569m of UK practice revenue is about £8.5m of revenue. At a 50 percent drop-through once rosters flex, that loss costs about £4.3m of EBITDA and about 4.5p of EPS: FY2027 EPS falls to about 88.8p (−4.8 percent) and EBITDA to about £144.5m (a 19.3 percent margin), below the comfort range. Before rosters flex (a 75 percent drop-through), the cost is about £6.4m of EBITDA and 6.8p of EPS, taking EPS to about 86.5p. The lower base carries into FY2028 (EPS about 97p against 102p). If volume falls only 1.0 percent, because the Advanced tier and the cohort arrive early, the same arithmetic gives FY2027 EPS of about 97.8p, above consensus. Watch: Healthy Pet Club members (500,000 is the alarm level), the Advanced tier count at the interims (25,000 is the test) and practice LFL growth against 1.0 percent.

Judgement 2: UK price growth (4.0 percent) matches wage growth (3.6 percent gross, 3.0 percent net of productivity) but does not beat it. If competition and published prices force price growth down to 3.0 percent with no volume relief, the lost point on £569m is about £5.7m of revenue, almost all of it margin: about £5.8m of EBITDA and 6.2p of EPS, taking FY2027 EPS to about 87.1p (−6.6 percent). If wages rise 4.6 percent (1 point higher) on about £305m of UK practice staff cost, EBITDA falls about £3.1m (about £3.7m group-wide), or 3.3p to 3.9p of EPS, taking EPS to about 89.5p to 90p. If price growth holds at 4.5 percent and volume falls only 1.5 percent, EPS gains about 3p from each, reaching about 99p. Watch: the clinical staff ratio (34.3 percent of revenue in H2 FY2026) and non-clinical cost of sales (21.4 percent) at the interims.

Judgement 3: the R&D credit resets to £12.5m. This judgement is where we differ most from the company's comfort with consensus. If the £6.6m release repeats, EPS gains 7.0p and FY2027 EPS reaches about 100p, a beat; but only £2.9m of the provision remains, so a full repeat is unlikely. If CVS recognises only the in-year run-rate of about £11m, EPS loses 1.6p. If the government removes or restricts the R&D regime (a low probability inside 18 months, but a policy decision that could arrive suddenly at a fiscal event), EBITDA loses about £12.5m and EPS about 13p after tax: FY2027 EPS falls to about 80p (−14 percent), and the margin excluding the credit is 17.6 percent. If HMRC (the UK tax authority) disallows part of the £38.3m of open claims, the hit lands first on cash and reported earnings and could add up to about 0.3x to leverage; we put the probability of a material hit to adjusted EBITDA inside 18 months at about 10 percent, and of a cash clawback at about 15 percent. CVS's recognition discount on the FY2026 claim (about 7.6 percent) is far below VetPartners' 50 percent, so CVS's accounting for the credit sits at the aggressive end of peer practice. Watch: the H1 credit in the interim notes; above £7m signals a repeat, and below £5.5m signals a problem.

Judgement 4: acquisitions continue at about £50m a year at multiples rising from 6.2x to 7.5x, and buybacks resume modestly. Each £10m not deployed costs about 0.5p of EPS in the first year and about 1p annualised. Each turn of multiple above 6x on £50m of acquisitions costs about £1.2m of EBITDA and about 0.5p of EPS a year, cumulatively. Removing every unannounced acquisition and buyback puts FY2029 EPS at about 103p and EBITDA at about £155m, against our 112.9p and £171.9m (−9 percent). That 103p is also about 8 percent below the 112p consensus, so consensus FY2029 already depends on acquisitions that brokers do not itemise.

Smaller variations of judgement 4 are also sized. Halving the acquisition pace from FY2028 costs about 1p of EPS in FY2028 and about 3.5p in FY2029. Australian multiples of 7.5x rather than 6.5x cost about 0.5p a year, compounding to about 2p by FY2030. No buyback renewal costs about 1p in FY2029 and about 5p by FY2031; a £30m-a-year programme adds about 1p to 2p in FY2029 and about 8p by FY2031, because each £10m retires about 0.75m shares, about 1.1 percent of the total. Watch: sites and consideration at each update (less than £15m of Australian consideration since July by March would be a warning), the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) merger register, and the new chief executive's first capital-allocation statement.

Judgement 5: the multiple (treated in #11). Each turn of the two-year-forward P/E on about 105p of forward earnings is worth about 105p of share price, or about 8 percent. The move from 12.4x to the 14.92x guideline is worth about 265p, about 20 percent, which is more than every earnings judgement above combined.

Our FY2027 earnings range (the cone) runs from about 82p to about 104p, centred on 92p to 96p. The 82p downside combines UK volume of −3.5 percent on 3.5 percent price, wage inflation of 4 percent, an R&D credit of £10m, acquisitions of £25m a year at 6.5x to 8x, and no new buyback. The 104p upside combines UK volume of −1.5 percent on 4.5 percent price, a repeat of the R&D release, acquisitions at 6x to 7x and £30m a year of buybacks. For FY2028 the range is about 81p to 121p. Our probability distribution for FY2027 EPS is: below 88p, 15 percent; 88p to 92p, 25 percent; 92p to 96p, 40 percent; 96p to 100p, 15 percent; above 100p, 5 percent (Figure 30). Over 18 months the range is roughly symmetric in pence, but the near term is tilted down.

Against the market. We are below consensus for FY2027 EBITDA for reasons already in the annual report, and above it on the share count. We are neutral for FY2028, and above consensus from FY2029 because we model the acquisitions the company says it will make. We agree with consensus that the margin stays about 20 percent and that organic growth is 2 to 3 percent.

Conclusion: our forecasts show adjusted EPS compounding at 9 to 11 percent a year (double digit from FY2029) on revenue growth within the historical range and a margin that barely moves, because CVS buys its growth and divides it over fewer shares rather than earning it through a better operating business.

Score: 75, set by the Rater. The roughly 10% a year sits at the very bottom of the 10-15% B band (consensus next-year growth 8.5%, 36th percentile, is lower still), and it is bought and divided rather than earned: margin flat at about 20%, UK organic core unchanged, the R&D credit stepping down, so I place it at the floor of the band.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

The next six months are more likely to bring small estimate cuts and soft optics than upgrades; the upgrade cycle, if it comes, starts with the FY2027 results and the new chief executive's plan in the second half of 2027.

The three events before April 2027 will look soft. The four-month update (late November), the H1 trading update (January) and the interim results (4 Mar 2027) will show group LFL growth of about 1.5 percent against 2.7 percent and an H1 margin flat at about 19 percent. In March they will also show an H1 R&D credit of about £6m against about £7.1m.

FY2027 consensus EPS is likely to drift down to 92p to 94p by March, which is where our forecast sits. Three forces will push FY2027 consensus EBITDA down by £1m to £3m between now and March: the R&D credit, the LFL optics and the flat H1 margin. One force will push consensus EPS up 1 to 2 percent: brokers truing up the share count to 66.3m.

FY2028 consensus is more likely to be held than cut. FY2028 consensus (£158m of EBITDA, 104p of EPS) needs about 3 percent organic growth and a held margin on top of acquisitions. Brokers who exclude unannounced acquisitions (Jefferies, with FY2028 revenue of £770m) will hold their numbers; brokers who include them will add to their numbers as CVS announces acquisitions. Shore Capital's flat FY2028 EPS forecast (95.4p) is the outlier that will be revised up on any growth.

Out-year consensus is more likely to be upgraded than cut. FY2029 consensus rests on six brokers and FY2030 consensus on two. As CVS demonstrates the £50m acquisition pace each half and brokers clean up the depreciation artefact, out-year estimates should rise.

Pets at Home will set the tone for UK volume assumptions. Pets at Home's vet revenue grew 1.9 percent in the first quarter of its FY2027, and it guides to low-single-digit vet growth. Its interim results on 25 Nov will shape investors' UK volume assumptions for both companies.

Inference. The scope for upgrades over the next six months is low, and the scope for small cuts is real. Over twelve months the picture flips: the FY2027 results in September 2027 (H2 LFL growth against an easy comparative, with the full year landing at the bottom of the range) and the new chief executive's first plan mark the turn. The sell-side's ratings are ahead of its estimates: 73 percent of ratings are Buy, the median target is 22 percent above the price and the revision score is +5, yet EPS revisions are flat to −1 percent. That configuration resolves either through estimates catching up or through targets coming down. We expect targets to hold through March on hopes for the appointment, and to be tested in September.

So what. We assign three probabilities to where consensus ends the next 18 months (Figure 33): FY2027 EPS consensus below 94p, about 60 percent; FY2028 EPS consensus within 2 percent of 104p, about 55 percent; FY2029 EPS consensus above 112p, about 55 percent. We expect the net breadth of revisions to be small negative in November, negative in January and mixed in March (EBITDA down 1 to 2 percent, EPS flat, out-years up for brokers that add acquisitions), then neutral to positive from September 2027 if H2 LFL growth is 3 percent or more. A narrative upgrade, if it comes, will come from the appointment plus a credible reset, not from higher numbers.

Strongest counter-case. The appointment lands before March with a respected operator, the November update discloses practice LFL growth separately and it is above 2 percent, and Pets at Home's care-plan print on 25 Nov supports the Advanced tier story. Targets would then rise on the narrative before the numbers move. That sequence is the one route to an early re-rating, and it is plausible but not probable.

What would change my view. A November update reporting group LFL growth above 2.5 percent, which would imply practice LFL growth near 2 percent, would move our FY2027 EPS towards 96p and the breadth of revisions to neutral four months early.

Against the market. Deutsche Bank expects consensus to remain unchanged after the results and says the headwinds are fully discounted; Jefferies wants evidence on routine visits and client retention before moving. We think both brokers will trim FY2027 EBITDA by about 1 percent by March, and that neither has modelled the H1 margin on a like-for-like credit basis. We agree that FY2028 consensus is attainable.

Conclusion: the next six months are more likely to bring small cuts and soft optics than upgrades, and the upgrade cycle, if it comes, starts with the FY2027 results and the new chief executive's plan in the second half of 2027.

Score: 37, set by the Rater. Guidance is more likely trimmed to the bottom of the comfort range (30%) or reset by the incoming chief executive (60% for the LFL framework) than raised (10%), and FY2027 consensus EPS is likely to drift from 95p to 92-94p by March on the R&D release, soft LFL optics and a flat H1 margin, a small cut against about 6% revenue growth, with only out-year and narrative upgrades (deals, a credible appointment) in the twelve-month window; that is less negative than D'Ieteren's cuts but below Alfen, coherent with the group's 36.

#8 Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative and the share price, and at peers

CVS has no momentum of the kind the framework rewards: guidance and estimates are flat, the share price has stalled, and the sector's strength has not reached a stock that moves 87 percent on its own news.

Guidance momentum: none. CVS reaffirmed its guidance rather than raising it, and let one ambition, the doubling of EBITDA, slip by a year.

Sell-side momentum: flat estimates, rising ratings. On FactSet data at 29 Oct 2026, FY2027 EPS revisions are 0, −1 and 0 percent over one, three and six months; EBITDA revisions are zero throughout; sales revisions are +1 percent; and the mean target price has moved −1 percent. The share of Buy ratings is 73 percent, up 9 points over six months. The dashboard's revision-momentum score is +5 (−5 in July), and the dashboard's sell-side earnings momentum rating is D.

Narrative momentum: stalled. The regulatory clearing that the market waited three years for arrived in March and September 2026 without a re-rating. The investor narrative around CVS is about capital returns (Converium, Kelso). The sector narrative is about take-privates (Spire at about 9x EBITDA, Qiagen, DCC Healthcare, Animalcare, Dechra) and the earnings of the Nordic care companies. CVS is not where the sector's momentum is.

Technical momentum: constructive on the moving averages, middling on relative strength (Figure 34). At 1315p on 29 Oct, the price is 5.0 percent above its 200-day moving average, the 50-day average is above the 200-day, and the 200-day average has risen in 6 of the last 12 months. CVS's relative-strength percentile is only 52 of the universe, and the dashboard's technical momentum rating is D.

Co-movement: CVS trades on its own news. The peer basket explains 13 percent of CVS's daily share-price variance over the latest six months (correlation 0.36, beta 0.48). That share has never exceeded 22 percent in any window, and it was about zero from October 2025 to March 2026.

Peers: the strength is elsewhere (Figures 38 and 39). Technical momentum is rated A or B at Ambea, Attendo, Humana, Medicover, Spire and Fresenius Medical Care. The Nordic care names are up 47 to 72 percent in twelve months, while Terveystalo is down 31 percent and Emeis down 24 percent. Pets at Home, which is not in the peer basket, trades at about 11.5x calendar 2026 earnings; Deutsche Bank values its vet division at about 14x, and its vet growth has slowed to 1.9 percent.

Inference. CVS has no momentum of the kind Richard's framework rewards. There are no guidance upgrades, and estimates are flat. The share price recovered from 8x to 12x earnings on the removal of a tail risk and then stalled. The technical picture is constructive on the moving averages but middling on relative strength. The sector's strength (a defensive bid and a take-private wave) is real but has not reached CVS, and on the co-movement evidence it will not reach CVS by osmosis. The one improving momentum reading is the share of Buy ratings, which is the sell-side betting on a re-rating ahead of the numbers.

So what. Do not expect the momentum ratings to help the case before mid-2027. The shares will trade on their own dates: 5 Nov (the rates decision), late November (the CVS update and Pets at Home's interims), January, 4 Mar, and the appointment, which is the only unscheduled one.

Strongest counter-case. Three signals suggest the bottom is in: the 50-day average has crossed above the 200-day, the six-month return is +12.4 percent, and the share of Buy ratings has risen 9 points. In a risk-off, rates-led market, the sector's defensive bid (our Fitness for Fighting tilt has the sector at Overweight) would amplify any company-specific catalyst.

What would change my view. Either a relative-strength percentile above 70 with the 200-day average rising in 9 of 12 months, or a revision-momentum score above +10 with EPS revisions positive over three months.

Against the market. We agree with the dashboard's D ratings for both technical and earnings momentum. We differ from the sell-side's implicit view that a re-rating is near: the breadth of revisions is more likely to tip negative into March than positive.

Conclusion: CVS's momentum is absent in guidance and estimates, flat in the share price and middling in relative strength, and the sector's strength is not a leading indicator for a stock that moves 87 percent on its own news.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Both measures are above 50, which gives B, but the sell-side score is carried by a 9-point rise in the buy share while EPS revisions are flat (0% over 3 and 6 months, 45th percentile), guidance was held not raised, the narrative has stalled after the CMA clearing and relative strength is barely positive, so the guidance, estimate and narrative parts strongly contradict the measures and move it one step to C, placed in the upper part of the band for the constructive moving averages (50-day above a rising 200-day).

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

CVS's earnings case is simple and lower-risk than the sector's, but its share price carries two sudden tails, the R&D credit and the leadership change, which must be carried as separate lines rather than inside the earnings range.

The case is simple: four monitorable lines carry the forecast. The four lines are the share count (monthly, through buyback announcements and total voting rights), acquisitions completed (at each update), and the clinical staff ratio and the R&D credit recognised (both half-yearly, at the interims). The perimeter is narrow: two countries, three segments, and one business model supplying about 91 percent of revenue.

The unpredictability is concentrated in one variable that CVS does not disclose directly: UK practice volume. CVS's trading updates give no split between price and volume, no split between acquired and organic growth, and no Australian LFL figure except annually. The capital side of the thesis traces line by line to EPS; the operating side (the 4 to 8 percent framework and the initiatives) does not trace at all.

The main fragility: two drivers can each be switched off by a single decision. The forecast has few independent sources of error to offset each other. A board decision on buybacks and acquisition pace, which will pass to an unnamed chief executive, could switch off one driver; a government policy decision on the R&D regime could switch off another.

Three further fragilities sit inside the numbers. First, the adjusted earnings line overstates economic earnings by roughly a third of the acquisition accretion, because contingent consideration tied to employment is excluded. Second, the margin target carries about 2 points of R&D credit that the company neither guides nor explains. Third, the swap expiry in February 2028 doubles the interest-rate sensitivity. The dashboard's riskiness rating is D; CVS's earnings are more predictable than a D implies, and its share price about as unpredictable.

Share-price risks: most are scheduled and trackable, and two sudden ones matter most (Figure 40). The scheduled risks (the three prints, the wage step and the swap expiry) can be planned around, although each print can move the shares 5 to 10 percent on the day in either direction. The semi-scheduled risks, the appointment and the first strategy update, are binary in direction but visible in advance. The sudden risks that matter most are a change to the R&D regime at a fiscal event and an HMRC disallowance of past claims; the other sudden risks are smaller or less likely. Covenant stress and renewed structural regulation are not plausible within the horizon.

Sector cyclicality: veterinary demand is defensive at the base and cyclical at the margin. Only 5.8 percent of owners say they would cut pet spending in a recession, and the companion-animal market grew 5.9 percent a year through 2007 to 2009. Yet US visits fell 3 percent in 2009 and 2 percent in 2010, and VCA posted eleven consecutive quarters of negative same-store sales before turning in the first quarter of 2011. UK pet spending fell 1 percent in 2025, and the 2022 to 2024 squeeze took CVS's practice LFL growth down to 1 percent.

The precedents for CVS's multiple are brutal (Figure 41). A wage spike on a fixed cost base took CVS's P/E from 29x to 8.6x in 2017 to 2019. The CMA investigation, the cyber attack and payroll taxes took it from about 21x to 8x in 2022 to 2024. Peers show the same pattern: brokers cut Terveystalo's 2027 to 2028 estimates by 13 percent in one October 2026 note on volume; Spire fell about 25 percent on a trimmed outlook in March 2025; Monash IVF's profit fell 41 percent when volumes turned on a fixed cost base; and AddLife's return on capital fell below 8 percent on acquisition-led growth. CVS's own return on invested capital fell from 13.2 percent (FY2017) to 9.1 percent (FY2020) in its last acquisition-led phase.

The lesson: the market does not reward acquisition-led EPS growth with a higher multiple until organic growth re-appears. Acquisition-led growth is deliverable. Historically, though, the re-rating trigger has been either an organic re-acceleration (CVS in 2019 to 2021, on high-single-digit LFL growth) or a bid (VCA, Greencross, Spire).

The trough: a fair trough implies a fall of 13 to 19 percent, and deeper stress cases are unlikely now the regulatory tail has gone (Figure 42). The fair trough applies the ten-year 10th-percentile P/E of 10.9x to 24-month-forward EPS, either at consensus (105.2p) or 7 percent lower (98p). CVS's own acquisition price for small Australian practices, 6x FY2027 EBITDA, gives a similar value.

Against the market. The market treats the case as riskier than its earnings warrant (an 11.6x multiple, a D riskiness rating) and less risky than its near-term optics warrant (73 percent Buy ratings going into three soft prints). We think CVS's earnings range (about ±12 percent over 18 months, with a 60 percent chance of landing within ±5 percent) is narrower than Terveystalo's or Spire's because so much of the growth is transacted, and that its skew is milder because the 2024 to 2026 shocks are already in the base.

Conclusion: CVS offers a simple, concentrated and monitorable case whose earnings risk is lower than the sector's but whose share-price risk over the next six months is high, with two tails (the R&D credit and the leadership change) that must be carried as separate lines rather than inside the earnings range.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The earnings case is simple and narrow (four monitorable lines, growth largely transacted, FY2027 cone 82-104p around 93p with 60% inside 5%, leverage 1.63x against a 3.25x covenant, defensive demand), but the share price carries binary tails (the chief executive appointment, an R&D credit worth about 13p subject to policy and HMRC, three soft prints) and a history of brutal de-ratings (29x to 8.6x, 21x to 8x); slightly below the groups' 60 and 64 for that share-price fragility, below Shell and above Nexans.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

CVS is in late Bottoming: the earnings have turned up but the narrative has not, so the next six months test patience and the following twelve are the window.

The dashboard's rule puts CVS in the Bottoming phase (Stage 2, bucket B_early, on a two-year-forward P/E of 11.58x).

The earnings have turned. Adjusted EPS rose 6.9 percent in FY2026 after three years of decline, and a further 9 percent rise in FY2027 is mostly already in hand.

The multiple has bottomed. The two-year-forward P/E has risen from 8.2x (December 2024) to 12.4x. The share price set its 52-week low of 1,062p in March 2026, and the 50-day moving average is above the 200-day.

The narrative has not turned. CVS shows no organic inflection (LFL growth 2.1 percent, Healthy Pet Club membership falling), has no chief executive, has not raised guidance and has flat estimates. The breadth of revisions is about to tip negative, and the regulatory clearing is already spent.

The timing is uneven. The scope for upgrades lies in the out-years, not in the next two prints. The risks are front-loaded (three soft prints, the appointment), while the structural helps are back-loaded (the easy H2 comparative, annualising acquisitions, the pandemic cohort and a buyback renewal).

Inference. CVS is in late Bottoming, with the earnings leg already Turning Up and the narrative leg not yet. It is not Stalling, because earnings are rising and the balance sheet is comfortable; it is not Collapsing; and it is not yet in Thesis Broadening, which needs volume growth or a bid. The transition to Turning Up, in the framework's sense, requires the two company events: a named chief executive with a credible plan, and an LFL print of 3 percent or more. The most likely window for both is March to September 2027.

So what. Richard's framework rewards buying where the probability of upgrades is unusually skewed to the positive. That skew is not present today. It is likely to be present after the three prints, provided the January update does not reveal a volume step-down. The sequence of events matters more than the level of the shares.

Strongest counter-case. The appointment comes in December with a well-regarded operator, and the stock moves to Turning Up on the narrative alone, before the prints, as Pets at Home did when it named James Bailey (December 2025) ahead of the evidence. The cost of waiting would then be missing the first 10 to 15 percent of the move.

What would change my view. The appointment, in either direction; a January H1 EBITDA indication below £70m (Stalling risk); or a practice LFL print above 3 percent (Turning Up confirmed).

Against the market. On its ratings the sell-side treats CVS as already Turning Up; on the multiple the market treats it as Bottoming. We side with the multiple.

Conclusion: CVS is in late Bottoming, with the earnings already turning up and the narrative waiting on two company events that are expected but not scheduled, which makes the next six months a test of patience and the following twelve months the window.

Score: 49, set by the Rater. Late Bottoming, as the memo and the computed phase say: earnings have turned (FY2026 EPS +6.9%, +9% in FY2027 mostly in hand) and the multiple has lifted from 8.2x, but the narrative has not turned, revision breadth is likely to tip negative over the next three prints and Turning Up needs two undated company events; like Linea Directa the improvement is not yet broadening, but earnings already rising put it a step above, just below Solid State's Bottoming-to-Turning.

#11 The fair multiple

14.92x is a fair and defendable multiple for the end of 2027 if CVS names a credible chief executive and prints 3 percent organic growth; weighted for the chance that those events slip, the fair multiple is nearer 13.5x, and a fall to 10.9x would come faster than a rise to 14.9x.

Where the multiple is today. CVS's two-year-forward P/E is 11.6x on the dashboard's monthly series (2 Nov), 12.4x on FactSet's weekly series (23 Oct) and 12.7x in the model (25 Oct). The three figures differ because they blend forward EPS differently and are taken on different dates, not because they reflect different views.

The multiple sits near the bottom of its own history (Figures 44 and 45). Over ten years, the 10th percentile is 10.9x (labelled "crash"), the 35th percentile 15.8x ("conservative"), the median 18.6x ("prudent"), the 75th percentile 24.6x and the 90th percentile 31.7x. The five-year median is 13.5x and the two-year median 12.2x. The multiple peaked near 29x to 30x in 2021, on LFL growth of 7 to 17 percent, and troughed at 8x in late 2024, during the CMA investigation.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a Bottoming stock is the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history: for CVS, 14.92x, 29 percent above the current 11.58x.

Peers do not supply a sector multiple. Peer P/E percentiles span the 5th (Diagnostyka) to the 94th (Emeis). Pets at Home trades at about 11.5x earnings, and Deutsche Bank values its vet division at about 14x.

Precedents show what does and does not re-rate a consolidator (Figure 46). Strategic resets and regulatory clearings do not re-rate consolidators on their own: Vimian traded at a 22 percent discount to its peer two months after its reset; Pets at Home traded at 12.6x to 13x during its turnaround; and CVS traded at 7.6x EV/EBITDA the day after the CMA's binding order. A verified organic re-acceleration does re-rate them: CVS's multiple rose to 23x in 2020.

Private markets and brokers value CVS higher than the public market does. Private transactions sit at 9x to 14x EBITDA, against CVS's 7x. Jefferies' downside scenario puts the multiple at 13.8x on lower earnings, and its base case applies a 30 percent discount to a discounted-cash-flow (DCF) valuation.

My view of the fair multiple: 14.92x is right for the 18-month column, and I would not move it. The guideline sits below the midpoint of the stock's five-year 25th-to-75th percentile range and below the ten-year "conservative" band. It is about where a UK healthcare-services operator should trade once its two specific worries are resolved, given 9 to 11 percent EPS growth, a 20 percent margin, 1.7x leverage and a private-market value above its public one. It is a Turning Up multiple, not a multiple for peak delivery.

Qualification 1: the path to 14.92x depends on CVS's own events. Reaching the guideline requires the appointment and an H2 FY2027 LFL print of 3 percent or more, not a sector re-rating. We put the probability of both landing by December 2027 at about 45 to 50 percent. A probability-weighted multiple at that date is therefore nearer 13.5x (the five-year median), which still gives a positive return (see #12).

Qualification 2: the multiple is more fragile below than above. A disappointing appointment or a volume step-down would take the multiple to 10.9x, a 12 percent fall from here, in a single print. A bid at 9x to 10x EBITDA would value the shares at 1,770p to 1,990p, about 17x to 19x FY2028 consensus earnings, so corporate action is the one route to the upper bands of the range.

Against the market. The consensus median target of 1,600p implies about 15x 24-month-forward earnings, in line with the guideline; the two Hold targets (1,250p to 1,400p) imply 12x to 13x. We are with the guideline on the destination and with the Holds on the timing.

Conclusion: 14.92x is a fair and defendable multiple for the end of 2027, conditional on the appointment and an organic print of 3 percent or more; weighted for the probability of those events, the fair multiple is nearer 13.5x, and the downside to 10.9x would arrive faster than the upside to 14.9x.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Cheap on both measures gives A, but the cheapness is partly deserved: the ten-year range includes 29x peaks earned on high-single to double-digit LFL that the stalled, bought-growth business no longer has, the peer reading only just crosses the 15% line and adjusted EPS runs far above reported, so I place it at the floor of the band, supported by EV/EBITDA of about 7x against private deals at 9-14x.

#12 Total shareholder return

The modelled return is +38 percent to December 2027, but only about 10 points of it is earnings we can defend; the probability-weighted return is nearer +25 percent, with a floor of about +10 to +17 percent if CVS delivers its numbers and nothing else happens.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple (Figure 47). The model starts from a price of £13.17 and a two-year-forward P/E of 12.7x today, and assumes the multiple reaches 14.92x at the 18-month column.

What drives the return. The December 2027 value of £18.14 is 14.92x applied to the model's two-year-forward EPS at that date, a blend of FY2029 (114p) and FY2030 (128p) worth about £1.21. Today's price is 12.7x applied to a blend of about £1.04. The template splits the return into three legs. The earnings leg (+9.3 points to December 2027, +24.7 to June 2029) is the growth in forward earnings over the holding period. The multiple leg (+25.3 and +30.3) is the move from 12.7x to 14.92x. The dividend leg (+0.7 and +2.3) is a 9.5p to 10.5p dividend, a yield under 1 percent. The multiple therefore supplies two-thirds of the 18-month return and nearly half of the three-year return.

How to read the return: the earnings leg is defensible, the multiple leg is a bet. We can defend the earnings leg on transacted facts: about 9 to 11 percent a year, with the buyback done, the acquisitions owned and the comparatives easing. The template's share-count convention flatters that leg by about half a point a year; on an average share count, earnings would be about 2 percent lower by FY2030. The multiple leg is a bet on two events that our analysis cannot forecast, with a probability of about 45 to 50 percent that both land by December 2027.

Scaling the model's value by the multiple gives the range of outcomes (Figure 49). At an unchanged 12.7x, the return of about +17 percent is the floor for a case that delivers its numbers but gets no credit for them. The template's own split, which attributes only 9.3 points to earnings, would put that floor nearer +10 percent; the gap reflects how the template allocates the interaction between earnings growth and the multiple. At 10.9x, the fair trough multiple, the return is roughly flat, which is what a delivered year with a disappointing appointment looks like.

The asymmetry is attractive, but collecting it requires surviving three soft prints. Over 18 months, the two outcomes of the appointment give about +38 percent and about 0 percent, around a central +25 percent.
